narration_use: reference only when drafting; required units must be derivable from the public B2 inputs (table + intent)
file_naming: one G1 per input contract; B1/B3/B4/B5 need separate drafts
intent: To illustrate that Japan's demographic challenge is the caregiving burden on its working-age population which hinders innovation, rather than a shortage of workers.

units.meaning: Japan still has a large working-age population: the age groups 20-64 sum to 14.677 table-value units, which is more than half (about 0.58) of the combined total across all age groups (25.393).

basis.note: Sum of value for age groups 20-24, 25-29, 30-34, 35-39, 40-44, 45-49, 50-54, 55-59, 60-64 for both Male and Female series.
Sum of value for all age groups 0-4 through 95-99 for both Male and Female series.

accepted_routes: The 20-64 age groups total about 14.7, more than half of the total table value.
Working-age people are the largest block: about 58 per 100 of all table-value units shown.
There is no small working-age pool; ages 20-64 make up the majority of the distribution.
units.visual_evidence_rule: The combined 20-64 age groups must be encoded as a single quantity or highlighted as a group, and the total across all age groups must be available for comparison.
units.temporal_anchor: The problem is not that Japan doesn't have working-aged people / there will long be millions and millions of workers.
units.reviewer_question: Should the video explicitly quantify the working-age pool as more than half of the shown population, or only imply that it is large?

units.meaning: The elderly population is substantial: ages 65+ sum to 6.428 table-value units, about 0.44 times the 20-64 working-age sum (14.677).

basis.note: Sum of value for age groups 65-69, 70-74, 75-79, 80-84, 85-89, 90-95, 95-99 for both Male and Female series.
Sum of value for age groups 20-24 through 60-64 for both Male and Female series.

accepted_routes: 65+ is about 44 per 100 of the working-age 20-64 total.
The elderly population is about 0.44 times the working-age population.
For every working-age person, there are roughly 0.44 elderly people.
units.visual_evidence_rule: The 65+ age groups must be visually separable from the 20-64 age groups, and their combined size must be comparable to the 20-64 combined size.
units.temporal_anchor: But they'll be busy caring for their parents.
units.reviewer_question: Is the elderly-to-working-age ratio the right way to convey caregiving burden, or is a simple count of elderly people enough?

units.meaning: The largest single age cohort is 45-49, totaling 2.050 table-value units (Male 1.000 + Female 1.050), making it the peak of the age distribution.

basis.note: Male series value for age group 45-49.
Female series value for age group 45-49.

accepted_routes: 45-49 is the tallest age band, with a total of about 2.05.
The 45-49 cohort is the maximum of the distribution.
The peak age group is 45-49, slightly larger than 50-54.
units.visual_evidence_rule: The 45-49 age group must be visually identifiable as the tallest combined age band or as the maximum total.
units.temporal_anchor: working-aged people / busy caring for their parents.
units.reviewer_question: Should the video call out the specific peak age cohort (45-49), or is aggregate working-age enough?

weight_mode_note: every unit gets 1/n so coverage is a plain share; weight_template is kept for per-type analysis only
